source: Lin, Snell, Packer et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Closest LLM test of preplay for unpursued goals: a frozen model reasons over the context before any query arrives, then answers the later query from that precomputed text. Gain is larger when the future query is more predictable from the context.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; scaling sleep-time compute adds up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME). Predictability measured as log-probability of the question given the context under Llama2-70B base, split into 5 bins; accuracy gain rises with bin. o1 showed limited gain on AIME.
quote: sleep-time compute is most effective in settings where the question can be predicted from the context
limits: Predictability is the log-prob of the true question, not a goal-probability estimate made by the agent. Tasks are math with one fixed context. At high test-time budgets the test-time-only baseline is slightly better (less distracting text in the prompt).
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'precompute only for likely future queries': gain scales with predictability. Gives a measurable gate for a preplay step: skip it when goals are unpredictable.

source: Lin, Snell, Packer et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time: amortisation and agentic case study
finding: Precomputation pays back only when several queries share the context. Cost model weights a test-time token as 10x a sleep-time token.
numbers: Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: average cost per query falls 2.5x when sleep-time work is shared across related queries. With 1 or 2 questions per context sleep-time compute is less favourable than test-time only; with 5 or 10 it improves the cost-accuracy Pareto. SWE-Features agentic case: about 1.5x fewer test-time tokens at low budgets, but test-time-only wins at high budgets (higher precision, comparable recall).
limits: The 10x test-time price factor is a latency argument. At equal TOTAL tokens (no price weighting) the benefit shrinks; this is the exact comparison gap 5 asked for and the paper does not give it directly. F1 on predicted file set is a proxy metric.
agent_relevance: Answer to gap 5: preplay for unpursued goals breaks even only when each stored route is reused by several later tasks. Matches the map-vs-value boundary (goal recurrence).

source: Hu, Van Durme, Andreas, Jhamtani (2026 v2) Sample-Efficient Online Learning in LM Agents via Hindsight Trajectory Rewriting (ECHO)
finding: In-context hindsight relabeling works without any weight update: after a failed episode the frozen LM names goals the trajectory could have reached, writes an optimised trajectory for each, and stores compressed versions in a scratchpad. This is prompting only.
numbers: XMiniGrid-Stateful: 10 generated environments, 4 objects in 4 rooms, 16 sequential pick-up queries each, up to 64 steps, duplicates allowed. ECHO beat vanilla ReAct by 80% in average reward and the next best baseline (Reflexion, AWM) by 42%. PeopleJoinQA-Stateful (5 organisations, 248 queries): ECHO 4.6% below best accuracy (Reflexion) but AWM and ECHO used about 1.6 fewer messages per query; no method dominated in every organisation.
quote: ECHO outperforms vanilla language agent baselines by up to 80%
limits: One lab, own benchmarks made 'stateful'. Equal-token comparison was not reported. Gain is largest where rewards are sparse and the baseline is weak.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 2 in part: tagging stored runs with other achieved goals helps a prompted agent. It is hindsight over achieved goals, not weighted by future goal probability.

source: Hu et al. (2026) ECHO: trajectory validity of hindsight-imputed workflows
finding: Label noise was checked once: imputed workflows were given back to the agent to see if they reach the imputed goal.
numbers: 40 sampled XMiniGrid examples: 34 of 40 (85%) reached the imputed goal. Of 6 failures, 4 were agent deviations from the workflow and 2 were infeasible synthesized steps.
limits: No noise-injection sweep: nobody varied the share of wrong labels, so the breaking point is unknown. N=40, one environment family. The 15% failure includes execution errors, so label error alone is about 5% (2 of 40).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 noise question stays open, but a first number exists: about 5% bad labels (2/40) did not stop the gain. Add a verify-by-replay gate before storing a relabel.

source: Hu et al. (2026) ECHO: goal recurrence in the benchmark design
finding: ECHO's test sets goal recurrence by design: the same environment resets and a random object goal is asked 16 times with duplicates allowed, so earlier hindsight routes get reused.
numbers: 16 queries per environment over 4 objects, so on average each goal is asked 4 times. The recurrence rate, number of goals and switching rate were not varied.
limits: Recurrence is fixed, not an experimental factor, so the paper cannot say where hindsight memory stops paying. Same limit as for every LLM study found.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open as a controlled experiment. A cheap test for us: sweep goals-per-environment and repeat rate, compare route-per-goal memory with current-goal-only memory.

source: Li and Tao (2026) When Does Memory Help Multi-Trajectory Inference for Tool-Use LLM Agents?
finding: Memory is treated as in-context experience replay (no weight change). Four memory methods x three inference strategies x four tool-use benchmarks. Which memory helps depends on the inference method, so reported gains are partly a property of the search method.
numbers: Reflection reaches significance only under MCTS, not best-of-N. Atomic fact memory is accuracy-neutral but cuts trajectory length 19-26% on tasks with reusable environment structure (SQL list_tables skip rate 4% to 77%). Fact plus reflection together: skip rate 77% to 20% and pass@5 58.8% to 52.9% on WikiSQL (51 examples), 49.0% to 46.9% on WikiTQ.
limits: Verifier-free setting, Haiku 3.5 and Sonnet 4.6 policies, small example counts (51 WikiSQL; KGQA 150 or a 69-subset). Not a goal-recurrence design.
agent_relevance: Stored items can conflict: two memory types together did worse than one. A route store should hold one authoritative route per goal, not stacked notes.

source: Li and Tao (2026) memory cost accounting (Table 11 and appendix)
finding: Memory that needs an extra LLM call to write costs real tokens; memory that only injects raw observations costs nothing extra.
numbers: WikiSQL best-of-N, 51 examples: no memory 2.2M policy tokens, about $2; reflection 3.5M policy tokens plus 0.2M supervisor tokens, about $5; fact memory 1.6M policy tokens plus 0.2M supervisor, about $3. Total experiment about $1,384.
limits: Dollar costs use Bedrock prices that differ between policy and augmentor models, so they are not equal-token comparisons. Fact memory used fewer policy tokens than none.
agent_relevance: Part answer to gap 5: a memory write costs a modest extra call, and good memory can repay it by shortening later runs. No study gives a clean equal-total-token test for route precompute.

source: Reddy (2026) Selective Memory Retention for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (TraceRetain, ICML 2026)
finding: Bounded external memory for a frozen gpt-5-mini agent on ALFWorld. Eviction scores combine success, age, access frequency, redundancy, specificity, similarity and downstream utility. On clean streams all bounded policies matched unbounded memory.
numbers: Clean ALFWorld T=100 and T=200: bounded policies within Wilson 95% CIs of one another; memory beats no memory across two seeds. Held-out transfer: 47-49 of 50 tasks with memory vs 39 of 50 without. FIFO-K50 96/100 on clean stream.
limits: Saturated benchmark; two seeds. No goal-drift stream, and no 'need' term based on predicted future goals. Access frequency is the nearest proxy.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: nobody has tested need x gain eviction under goal drift. Simple heuristics suffice on a clean stream, so any gain from a goal-belief score must be shown under drift or noise.

finding: With 75% synthetic distractor writes, unbounded memory and FIFO retrieval quality collapse while score-based eviction holds.
numbers: Precision@5: unbounded 20.2% to 12.4%; FIFO-K50 15.8% to 3.8%; TraceRetain-CEM 16.9% to 16.6% and kept 97/100 task success. Unbounded memory had the highest similarity (0.87) but lowest precision: failed distractors sit close to the query in embedding space.
limits: Synthetic noise, seed 42, one benchmark. Differences between bounded policies on clean data are inside the CIs.
agent_relevance: A value-scored store protects retrieval from near-duplicate junk. Rank routes by value (reuse x success), not by similarity alone.

source: Bamidele (2026) AMV-L: Lifecycle-Managed Agent Memory for Tail-Latency Control
finding: Utility-scored eviction with exponential decay and tiered promotion versus TTL and LRU, in a serving system with fixed prompt-injection caps. The paper argues LRU can evict long-lived high-utility items after phase shifts.
numbers: Vs TTL: 3.1x throughput, latency down 4.2x (median), 4.7x (p95), 4.4x (p99); requests over 2 s from 13.8% to 0.007%. Vs LRU: +26% median and +3% p95 latency, -15% p99, 6% fewer tokens per request, retrieval value within 0-2%.
limits: Synthetic but controlled workload; measures latency and retrieval value, not agent task success. The phase-shift claim is argued, not tested as a separate drift condition in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Supports value-plus-decay eviction as a systems design, but gives no evidence on task success under goal drift (gap 10 stays open).

source: Kim, Lee, Park, Seo (2024, v4) How Language Models Extrapolate Outside the Training Data: The Case of Cognitive Maps
finding: Re-checked the 76.5% vs 19.0% claim and tested whether prompting alone can induce cognitive-map chain of thought. Result: it cannot, for the models tested in 2024.
numbers: Fine-tuned: optimal planning 19.0% (no CoT), 26.5% (best plain CoT), 76.5% (backward cognitive map with unmarking); reachable 32.1%, 33.9%, 88.5%. Exploration-only DFS reached 94.5% vs 88.5% for cognitive maps, but with quadratic step growth. Few-shot (100 gridworld items, 0 to 4 demonstrations): cognitive-map prompts gave 0-1% for Llama-3 8B/70B and GPT-4o and at most 10% in one cell; only GPT-o1 with plain prompting climbed (0, 18, 34, 38% at 0, 1, 2, 4 shots).
limits: PDF table text extracted with scrambled row labels, so one 10% cell is not safely assigned to a model. Models are mid-2024; no 2026 frontier model tested. Small toy gridworld.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the gain needs training. For a prompt-only scaffold, do not count on 'build a map first' prompts; test it. Plain DFS exploration beat the map in success rate.

source: Li, Zhu, Das, Dube (2026) Do LLMs Build Spatial World Models? Evidence from Grid-World Maze Tasks (ICLR 2026 workshop)
finding: Prompt-only test on 2026 frontier models (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-5-mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5, DeepSeek-Chat). Success depends on how the maze is written, not on a stable internal map.
numbers: Gemini 80-86% on 5x5 to 7x7 mazes with tokenized adjacency input vs 16-34% with visual grid text (2-5x gap). Reasoning traces covered 96-99% of the semantic content but did not give consistent spatial computation; models treated each question independently instead of building a cumulative map.
limits: Abstract page only (not full paper).  Only the abstract page was read, no cognitive-map prompt condition reported there, and no fine-tuning arm. Workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, second half: in 2026 models, a graph given as an adjacency list works; a free-form map in text does not. Feed the agent routes as explicit edge lists.

source: Webb et al. (2025, Nature Communications) Improving planning with large language models: a modular agentic architecture (MAP)
finding: Prompt-only brain-inspired planner (separate LLM modules for monitoring, predicting state, evaluating, decomposing, orchestrating; with tree search) improves multi-step planning with GPT-4 and no fine-tuning, including CogEval graph tasks where plain GPT-4 failed.
numbers: Valuepath 100% solved; Steppath perfect at 2 and 3 steps, near perfect at 4; no invalid actions. Tower of Hanoi 3 disks: nearly 7x the zero-shot solve rate, 100% when taking the best of 5 runs; average plan length 5.4 vs 4.4 optimal; OOD 4-disk problems solved while baselines scored near 0%. Reward Revaluation task only on par with baselines.
limits: GPT-4 era (2024 models); many LLM calls per problem, so not equal-token vs chain of thought. The authors note limits of prompting and suggest fine-tuning modules.
agent_relevance: Counter-point to Kim 2024: a prompt-only scaffold with separated predict/monitor modules can plan on graphs. The Reward Revaluation case (goal value changes) is the one it did not fix, which is the map-vs-value test.

source: Mallory, Widloski, Foster (2026 preprint) Spatial goals trap hippocampal replay (full text)
finding: Read the full results. Rats foraged in a 90x90 cm arena with nine wells; reward at one fixed Goal well on odd trials and at a random Non-Goal well on even trials. Replay at the Goal was slower, shorter and ended near the Goal.
numbers: N=4 rats, 44 sessions (39 sessions from 3 rats for the delayed-reward variant); 1,960 Goal stops, 1,939 Non-Goal stops. Population-event rate at Goal about 2x Non-Goal (Z=5.4, p=5.7e-8). Remote replays terminate at the Goal more than at a distance-matched well (Z=3.7, p=2.4e-5). Replay path speed slower (Z=-4.6), net displacement smaller (Z=-5.1). Attractor network with weaker spike-frequency adaptation at the Goal reproduced it (replay length vs adaptation r=0.997, 4 points).
limits: Goal was fixed within each session and changed only between sessions, so goal switching (Sagiv's p11 prediction) was NOT tested. No bottleneck analysis. Does not mention Sagiv et al. N=4 rats, one lab. Page text read up to 100,000 of 132,521 characters.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 still open. Adds a third explanation family (adaptation-based local trapping) that predicts replay piling up at the current goal, the opposite of a goal-general map's spread over goals.

source: Search note (this session): independent replication of HSL and AgentHER
finding: A web search for independent replications of hindsight relabeling for LLM agents, and for results on larger models, returned only the original HSL paper and summaries of it. No independent lab result found.
numbers: HSL ALFWorld-unseen figures appear as 92.5% (DPO+HSL, 800 demonstrations) and 97.76% (SFT+HSL, single run) in different places; WebShop 70.28 on one aggregator vs 66.97 in the paper table, so numbers differ by source and variant.
limits: Absence of evidence from one search; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited, so forward-citation lists could not be pulled. Snippet-level only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. ECHO (different lab, different method, prompting) agrees in direction but is not a replication of the training results. Treat HSL and AgentHER gains as single-source.

source: Search note (this session): LLM-agent studies that weight stored routes by future-goal probability
finding: Searches (web plus Semantic Scholar title queries) for prioritised or goal-belief-weighted memory for LLM agents found only hindsight relabeling (ECHO, HSL, AgentHER, SAC-GLAM), value-scored eviction (TraceRetain, AMV-L) and query-predictability-gated precompute (sleep-time compute). None weights routes by an estimated P(future goal).
numbers: Zero studies found among the titles scanned; several Semantic Scholar queries were rate limited (HTTP 429) and not read.
limits: Weak absence evidence: coverage limited by rate limits. Terms used: prioritized replay, hindsight, goal distribution, future tasks, memory eviction.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open and is a real research gap. The nearest tests are sleep-time compute (predictability gating) and TraceRetain (value-scored eviction); a direct P(goal) x gain score is untested.

source: Search note (this session): can an LLM estimate P(future goal) from task history; slow versus fast estimate
finding: No study found that asks an LLM agent to output a goal-probability distribution from its own history and scores calibration, nor one that compares slow and fast goal-estimate updating. The only indirect measure is log-probability of the real next query given context (sleep-time compute) which tracked payoff.
numbers: Sleep-time compute used Llama2-70B base log-probability across 5 predictability bins; no calibration or Brier score reported.
limits: Log-probability is a score of a known query, not a stated belief about goals. Search coverage limited by rate limits.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. A pilot would log the agent's stated P(goal) per task and score it with Brier loss against the next goal, with two update rates (fast and slow).

source: Search note (this session): rodent or human tests of the bottleneck and goal-switching-order predictions
finding: One web search for new data on bottleneck-state replay and goal-switching order found none. Results listed: the Sagiv map-building preprint (June 2025), the Widloski/Foster rerouting work, a Nov 2025 van der Meer seminar abstract saying paradoxical replay may prevent interference between competing traces.
numbers: No numbers; seminar and listing text only.
limits: Snippet-level; a second planned search was blocked by the shared search budget. Mallory 2026 (opened above) is the newest dataset checked and does not test either prediction.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 7 stay open. The cheapest separating experiment: switch the rewarded arm at a known rate within session and check whether replay order follows P(switch) (map), stays at the current goal (value), or stays at the other arm (protection).
